title: Redwood Private VPC security architecture deep dive with Celeste Trust
summary: Deep dive on Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) deployment options and network isolation: ingress/egress patterns, firewalling, NAT, and peering. Reviewed KMS/CMEK ownership, SOC 2/ISO evidence, RBAC/SSO (SAML/SCIM), audit log integration with SIEM, and data residency concerns. Agreed next steps to share architecture diagram, SOC2 pack, and schedule on-prem install call.
next_steps: Redwood: Send Private VPC architecture diagram and YAML of recommended security group rules (Maya)
Redwood: Provide SOC 2 / ISO27001 evidence pack and security whitepaper (Jordan)
Customer: Share network CIDR ranges and preferred peering method (Liam)
Schedule on-prem installation planning call with Celeste infra team (Ravi to propose times)
action_items: Maya - email architecture diagram and SG/NACL YAML by 2026-07-21
Jordan - upload SOC2/ISO evidence pack and HSM/KMS integration notes by 2026-07-22
Liam - share VPC CIDRs and approved egress list by 2026-07-23
Marcus - gather firewall appliance version and proxy termination details by 2026-07-24
transcript:
00:00 Maya Patel: Good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. We wanted to do a deep dive on the Private VPC and on-prem security architecture with Celeste, make sure we map to your compliance controls. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Jordan and Ravi from our security/infra team are here.
00:18 Liam O'Connor: Thanks Maya. We have Ayesha (CISO) on the call, Marcus from network, and Priya from compliance. Main ask — how do you isolate traffic, what controls live in our VPC vs Redwood managed components, and what's the path for audit logs and key ownership.
00:36 Jordan Kim: Great. We'll start with a high level, then get into ingress/egress, firewalling, and KMS. Quick note — apologies in advance if I say K-V cache instead of KV cache, and Redwood Private sometimes gets shortened to "Private VPC" — side effects of many calls.
00:54 Maya Patel: First slide — deployment modes. For Private we run a customer-dedicated control plane (customer-managed network) and an optional on-prem package for air-gapped setups. For VPC deployments we typically use VPC peering or PrivateLink depending on your network constraints.
01:12 Ayesha Rahman: Can you clarify what "customer-managed network" means — does Redwood need inbound access into our subnet? We can't have unsolicited ingress.
01:25 Ravi Desai: Short answer: no unsolicited ingress. The control plane endpoints are customer-facing but secured behind private endpoints (PrivateLink or VPC endpoints). For the optional control plane we provide a small control-plane image that can run in your management VPC and communicates outbound to Redwood for telemetry via egress only, or stays fully local for air-gapped.
01:47 Marcus Li: So all comms are outbound from our side? What about model updates or support tunnels?
01:55 Jordan Kim: By default the nodes initiate outbound connections to a Redwood endpoint — HTTPS/TLS on port 443 — and we use short-lived mTLS certs for node authentication. If you want, we can establish a customer-initiated VPN for support sessions or use a jumpbox approach — it never requires inbound holes in your public subnets.
02:16 Priya Shah: How do you handle egress filtering? We need to ensure tokens or secrets don't leave to arbitrary destinations.
02:23 Maya Patel: We recommend restricting egress to a small set of Redwood-managed FQDNs/IPs; we provide a JSON/YAML allowlist you can plug into firewall or proxy. We also support forced proxying through your corporate FW so egress is centrally logged.
02:39 Marcus Li: What about NAT vs IGW? We run private subnets with NAT — will Redwood nodes need public IPs?
02:47 Jordan Kim: No public IPs required. Nodes live in private subnets with a NAT gateway for outbound to Redwood endpoints. Alternatively, we can do VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink to avoid NAT and keep traffic on the AWS backbone. For on-prem, we support direct peering or a connector that tunnels to the control plane.
03:03 Ayesha Rahman: Encryption questions — CMEK or do you hold keys?
03:09 Ravi Desai: We support both. Customer Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) using your KMS (Cloud KMS or HSM) is supported for model artifact at rest and for secrets. For hosted control plane scenarios you can provide a key and rotate. For full on-prem or air-gapped installs you keep keys locally — Redwood can be configured to use a KMIP-compatible HSM if needed.
03:30 Priya Shah: Are audit logs immutable and do they include per-request metadata?
03:36 Jordan Kim: Yes, audit logs capture per-request metadata: timestamp, principal, route/model, decision/fallback, latency, token consumption approx., and any policy reasons. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via syslog or S3 ingestion. We also support writing to CloudWatch/Stackdriver. Retention/immutability is handled by your storage — e.g., S3 Object Lock for WORM if you need regulatory retention.
03:58 Liam O'Connor: For SOC 2 and ISO evidence, do you have that packaged?
04:04 Maya Patel: Yes, Jordan will send the SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 evidence pack. We also have our security whitepaper that maps controls to common frameworks.
04:12 Ayesha Rahman: RBAC and SSO — we need SCIM for provisioning and SAML for SSO, role separation, and least privilege.
04:22 Jordan Kim: We support SAML2.0 and SCIM provisioning for groups/roles, and you can map IdP groups to Redwood roles. For private deployments the console can be fronted with your IDP via an internal SAML endpoint. Role-based access controls are fully supported and can be integrated with your LDAP/Okta.
04:42 Marcus Li: What about network-level segmentation between services — inference nodes vs control plane?
04:48 Ravi Desai: Best practice is to put inference nodes in separate subnets, hardened with security groups that only allow traffic from your application subnets and the control-plane subnet. Control plane components live in a management VPC with restrictive egress. We recommend host-level firewall rules and disabling unnecessary outbound ports.
05:07 Maya Patel: We also recommend a dedicated logging VPC or S3 bucket for logs, and a transit gateway for centralised routing if you have multiple accounts.
05:15 Priya Shah: Firewalling question — do you recommend stateful SGs or external appliances?
05:21 Jordan Kim: Both are common. For strict compliance many customers put a NGFW (Palo Alto, Check Point) in front of the management VPC and use security groups for microsegmentation. We provide an SG/NACL baseline — e.g., allow HTTPS to Redwood endpoints, SSH only to bastions, no direct DB access. We'll send the exact YAML for firewall rules.
05:42 Liam O'Connor: How do you handle software updates/patches — we can't have automatic outbound fetching of large model blobs without approval.
05:51 Ravi Desai: We support a pull model where your infra pulls approved model artifacts from a signed Redwood artifact repository, or we can pre-seed artifacts via offline transfer for air-gapped installs. Updates require signed manifests and optional approval gating.
06:08 Ayesha Rahman: Does Redwood store PII? We need clear data residency guarantees.
06:14 Maya Patel: Data residency for request/response payloads is configurable — you choose the region for storage and logs in Private. For on-prem, data never leaves your environment unless explicitly configured. For hosted+Dedic we have region pinning and contractual commitments.
06:28 Marcus Li: On the audit trail — can you push to our Splunk?
06:33 Jordan Kim: Yes — log forwarding to Splunk via HEC or syslog is supported. We can also ship structured events to Kafka if you prefer. Events include request metadata, model id/version, and policy decisions.
06:46 Priya Shah: What's the retention default?
06:49 Jordan Kim: Default retention is 90 days in the platform, but for Private you control retention. We recommend 1 year for production, with S3 lifecycle to cold storage for longer retention if required.
07:02 Liam O'Connor: Incident response — what hooks do you provide?
07:06 Maya Patel: We provide audit trails, exportable logs, and webhook/alerting for anomalous behavior. Our support plan includes an IR runbook, and for enterprise we can do joint playbook exercises.
07:18 Marcus Li: If we use PrivateLink, what's the IP addressing expectation?
07:21 Ravi Desai: PrivateLink uses ENIs in your VPC; you'll see endpoints with our service name. Alternatively VPC peering is IP-routed and you manage CIDRs. We'll provide recommended CIDR allocation to avoid collisions.
07:35 Ayesha Rahman: For KMS rotation — will rotation break anything?
07:38 Jordan Kim: We design for key rotation: keys are referenced by key-id and we provide a key-rotation guide; we support envelope encryption to minimize disruption. For HSM scenarios we do a key handshake during startup.
07:52 Priya Shah: Do you persist model prompts or do you have redaction options?
07:56 Maya Patel: You control retention and can enable automatic redaction of PII from logs and traces. For compliance we recommend token-level hashing for telemetry.
08:08 Liam O'Connor: Are there compliance artifacts for penetration testing?
08:11 Jordan Kim: Yes — we have pentest summaries and remediation logs; we can share higher-level reports under NDA.
08:17 Marcus Li: A specific ask — our firewall team needs the list of IPs/FQDNs and ports for allowlisting and the YML.
08:23 Maya Patel: We'll send that in the next 48 hours.
08:27 Ayesha Rahman: If we choose to go fully on-prem and air-gapped, what is the support model?
08:31 Ravi Desai: We offer a support tier for on-prem including remote install assistance (via customer-initiated tunnels), an onsite option for enterprise, and runbook handoffs. For air-gapped installs we provide signed images and a verification checklist; updates are via offline media or signed bundles.
08:51 Priya Shah: Any third-party dependencies we should be aware of?
08:54 Jordan Kim: The primary ones are container runtime, Linux OS patches, and optionally a supported HSM vendor. We document specific versions and compat matrix in the infrastructure guide.
09:03 Liam O'Connor: Pricing and SLA? Not deep now but we want to understand the commitment for dedicated vs on-prem.
09:08 Maya Patel: We'll follow up with pricing ranges for Dedicated capacity and an on-prem license fee, plus optional premium support. We'll include SLA targets for uptime and P99 latency on the doc.
09:22 Marcus Li: One more on network logging — do you recommend VPC flow logs and do you store them centrally?
09:27 Jordan Kim: Yes, VPC flow logs are recommended for network forensic and we suggest forwarding to your logging VPC. They complement our application-level audit logs.
09:35 Ayesha Rahman: Any residual concerns about cross-tenant data leakage?
09:39 Ravi Desai: For Private deployments each customer gets dedicated infra; we use exclusive namespaces and disk-level isolation. For multi-tenant hosted workloads we logically isolate but for Private you get physical separation if requested.
09:56 Maya Patel: Quick recap — we'll send architecture diagram, firewall YAML, SOC2/ISO pack, and schedule the on-prem planning call. Action items captured. Anything else?
10:07 Liam O'Connor: No, that's good. Thanks.
10:10 Ayesha Rahman: Thanks everyone.
10:12 Maya Patel: Alright we'll follow up via email with the docs and proposed times.
10:16 End of recording.
